newsitem.title: UK: Britain to review law after Fred West film plan.
newsitem.headline: Britain to review law after Fred West film plan.

text.p: The British government has said it is to review the law after a row over plans for a movie about the life of Fred and Rosemary West, the British couple who killed a series of women and girls to satisfy perverted sexual cravings.

In an unexpected statement, made on the New Year public holiday, the country's top judge said the government would review the law governing the duties of the Official Solicitor, the legal official in charge of the West estate.

The announcement by the Lord Chancellor, Lord Mackay, follows an outcry after the official solicitor, Peter Harris, decided to sell the rights to West's memoirs to a company which is set to make a film about his life.
The government has come under pressure from churchmen and members of parliament to stop the sale.
But in a statement on Tuesday, Harris said it was the Official Solictitor's legal duty to "maximise the financial return to the estate" on behalf of West's five surviving children.
The duties of the Official Solicitor include looking after the interests of children, the mentally ill and others who are unable to represent themselves in court proceedings.
But Gloucester MP, Douglas French, has bitterly criticised the sale, saying "common human decency" should be put before "commercial exploitation" in the West case.
Fred West was found hanged two years ago in a prison cell where he was awaiting multiple charges of murder.

Many of his victims' bodies were found buried in the garden and cellar of his home at 25 Cromwell Street in Gloucester, western England -- a building so notorious that officials not only knocked it down but ground its bricks into dust.
Rosemary is now serving 10 life sentences for murdering girls and young women.
In his statement on Tuesday, Harris confirmed reports that the London-based Portman Entertainment Group had acquired an option to make the movie about West and his wife.

The option includes access to tape recordings of police interviews with West, tapes of his favourite blue movies and pages of his memoirs written when awaiting trial. Legal sources said there was no suggestion in the statement that Harris had done anything illegal.
The statement gave no further details of how or when the review would be carried out. Nor did it say whether the review would have any bearing on the film deal.
